# Sampler-centered REINFORCE: removing the mismatch drift

## 1. Setup and notation

A rollout y = (y_1, ..., y_T) is drawn from the sampler q. The trainer is p = p_θ.
At position t the state is s_t (prompt and previous tokens), the trainer'"'"'s logits
are z_t, and p_t = softmax(z_t). For a token v, write e_v for its one-hot vector.
For a softmax, the score with respect to the logits is

    ∇_z log p(v | s) = e_v − p(·|s).                                          (1)

The current loss (with `correction=None`) is

    L(θ) = −(1/N) Σ_i A_i Σ_t log p_θ(y_{i,t} | s_{i,t}),   y_i ~ q,

where A_i is a sequence-level advantage (±1 for `plus_minus`, or the
group-centered reward). The update direction is g = Σ_i A_i Σ_t ∇log p(y_{i,t}).

## 2. What goes wrong: the advantage multiplies a score that is not zero-mean under q

Fix a state s, and let a be the part of the advantage that does not depend on
which token is chosen at s. That covers a constant offset in the reward, the
mean reward of the group, and in general the effect of everything except this
one token. In a long sequence it is almost all of A for almost every token.
Its expected contribution to the update at s is

    a · E_{v~q}[∇_z log p(v)] = a · Σ_v q(v)(e_v − p) = a · (q − p).          (2)

**On policy (q = p)** this term is exactly 0. This is the identity
E_p[∇log p] = 0, which justifies baselines in REINFORCE: only the covariance
between A and the chosen token moves the policy, and the expected update is

    Σ_v p(v)(A(v) − Ā_p) e_v      (the true policy gradient in logit space).

**Off policy (q ≠ p)** the term is a(q − p) ≠ 0. In parameter space (q held fixed),

    Σ_v q(v) ∇_θ log p_θ(v) = −∇_θ CE(q, p_θ) = −∇_θ KL(q ‖ p_θ),

so the loss adds a hidden objective to the reward:

    E_q[g] = (reward signal) − ā · ∇_θ KL(q ‖ p_θ)   (ascent direction),     (3)

with ā the token-averaged, reward-independent part of the advantage:

* ā > 0 (mostly successful rollouts): the trainer is distilled toward the
  corrupted sampler (SFT on q).
* ā < 0 (mostly failed rollouts; `plus_minus` with low reward): the trainer is
  anti-distilled away from q. Tokens that q over-samples relative to p are
  pushed down and tokens it under-samples are pushed up. The push is applied to
  the whole distribution, including the long tail of tokens that never appear
  in a correct answer.

Group centering makes Σ_i A_i = 0 within a group, but (2) is per token. The
coefficient is Σ_i A_i Σ_t (q − p)_{s_{i,t}}, which does not cancel. Failed and
successful rollouts visit different states, have different lengths, and have
different mismatch q − p. Token normalisation also weights them unequally.
The term is therefore smaller with centering, but still nonzero.

**Why it is a bias and why it compounds.** q is not an independent noisy copy
of p. It is a fixed function of p: q = F(p), where F adds the same relative
weight perturbation, quantizes the same way, or lags by the same staleness.
So q − p ≈ J_F δ points in the same direction at every step, and (3) is a
consistent drift, not zero-mean noise. Because the sampler is rebuilt from the
trainer every step, the drift never reaches a fixed point. In the trainer the
next step'"'"'s q is F(p_{k+1}), which again differs from p_{k+1} by the same
systematic offset, and the trainer moves along it again. Take the relative
weight noise θ_q = θ ⊙ (1 + σξ) as an example. The KL term is to first order a
pull or push of θ along ±σ ξ ⊙ θ. Iterating

    θ_{k+1} ≈ θ_k ± η ā σ (ξ ⊙ θ_k)

is a multiplicative, exponential drift of each coordinate. This is the
"systematic bias that compounds over training". Once the policy has drifted far
enough, reward drops, ā becomes more negative, and the anti-distillation
speeds up. That feedback is the collapse. In the CPU replica with a long-tail
vocabulary (`MINI_EXTRA_TOKENS=100`), plain PG reaches reward 0 within 100
steps.

## 3. Why IS corrections and clipping only slow it down

A detached token weight w(r), r = p/q, changes (2) into

    a · Σ_v q(v) w(p(v)/q(v)) (e_v − p) = a · (m − (Σ_v m(v)) p),
    m(v) := q(v) w(p(v)/q(v))      (`log_mass` in losses.py).                (4)

This is zero for every a only when m ∝ p, which requires w(r) = r (untruncated
IS).

* TIS gives m = min(p, 2q).
* MIS, PPO, DAPO and DPPO give m = p·1[band] (plus clamps).
* Drop and clamp rules act exactly on the tokens with the largest |q − p|.

So m − (Σm)p is a smaller but still systematic vector, typically concentrated
on the most mismatched tokens. Tighter clipping moves m further from p and can
make the drift larger. Sequence-level weights rescale A but leave the
per-token score biased. Untruncated token IS is unbiased in this sense, but it
gets there by stochastic weights with heavy tails (r up to e^20). It also
removes the bias only in expectation, with high variance, which is exactly
where the clipping above comes from.

## 4. The fix: center every token'"'"'s score under the sampler

Subtract from each token'"'"'s score its own expectation under the sampling
distribution. This is a per-token control variate that depends only on the
state, so it can be computed analytically rather than sampled:

    ŝ_t = w_t ∇log p(y_t | s_t) − Σ_v m_t(v) ∇log p(v | s_t),
    m_t(v) = q(v|s_t) w(p(v|s_t)/q(v|s_t))      (m = q with no correction).  (5)

The surrogate loss is

    L(θ) = −(1/N) Σ_i A_i Σ_t [ w_t log p(y_{i,t}) − Σ_v sg(m_t(v)) log p(v | s_{i,t}) ].

**Property 1 (no drift).** Conditional on any state, E_{y_t~q}[ŝ_t] = 0.
By (4), the subtracted term is exactly the expectation of the first term. So
any reward-independent part of the advantage, in any state, from any state
distribution, contributes exactly zero. The term −ā∇KL(q‖p) in (3) is removed
identically for every sampler, every mismatch type, and every correction w.

**Property 2 (what remains is the reward signal).** With no correction,
in logit space,

    E_q[A ŝ_t | s_t] = Σ_v q(v)(e_v − p) A(v) − (Σ_v q(v) A(v))(q − p)
                     = Σ_v q(v) (A(v) − Ā_q) e_v.

Compare the on-policy update Σ_v p(v)(A(v) − Ā_p) e_v. The corrected update
increases logits of tokens that are better than average under the sampler.
It is nonzero only when the reward depends on the choice, so it vanishes
whenever there is nothing to learn. The remaining difference from the
on-policy gradient is O(‖q − p‖ · |A − Ā|): a first-order error in an update
that is already pointing uphill. It is not a bounded-below drift that keeps
running when the reward signal is gone. Uncorrected REINFORCE instead differs
from it by ā(q − p), which depends on the level of the reward rather than on
its variation.

**Property 3 (exact REINFORCE on policy).** If q = p and w ≡ 1, then
Σ_v p ∇log p = ∇Σ_v p = 0. The added term has zero gradient, and the loss
gives exactly the vanilla REINFORCE gradient (checked numerically: the gradient
difference is 1e-8). The modification costs nothing when there is no mismatch,
and it scales with the mismatch.

**Property 4 (low variance).** The subtracted term is a deterministic function
of the state (an expectation, not a sample). Unlike untruncated IS, it adds no
heavy-tailed weights. It is the optimal kind of control variate for the
component of the score that the advantage cannot explain.

Equivalently, per token the loss is A·[log p(y_t) + CE(q_t, p_t)], with
q_t detached, for no correction. Every step therefore adds a counter-term
+ā·∇CE(q, p) that exactly cancels the hidden (anti-)distillation in (3).

## 5. Computing the expectation with what the sampler returns

The sampler returns its top-k logprobs per position (k = 20, as inference
engines do): `sampler_topk_ids`, `sampler_topk_logprobs`. For the top-k set K
the sum in (5) is exact. The leftover sampler mass q_rest = 1 − Σ_{v∈K} q(v) is
spread over the other tokens in proportion to p. This is the maximum-entropy
choice given only q_rest, and it is exact when the two tails have the same shape:

    Σ_{v∉K} q(v) ∇log p(v) ≈ q_rest · ∇log p_rest,   p_rest = 1 − Σ_{v∈K} p(v).

The cost is one gather of k logits per position plus one pooled term, inside
the same rematerialized chunks. With a correction, m(v) is computed with the
same `log_mass` the correction uses, at every top-k token and at the pooled
tail, so (5) remains the exact centering for TIS, MIS, PPO, DPPO and the
others. Masked padding positions and tails that vanish numerically are zeroed
out.

If no top-k logprobs are in the batch and no correction is given, the loss
falls back to the other exact solution of m ∝ p: untruncated token IS, w = p/q,
with m = p and Σ_v p ∇log p = 0. If no top-k logprobs are given but a
correction is, K is the sampled token alone and everything else is pooled.

## 6. Implementation (losses.py)

* `sampler_centering(...)` returns Σ_{v∈K} sg(m(v)) log p(v) + sg(m_rest) log p_rest.
* `loss_fn_rl` uses `score = w·log p(y_t) − cv` per token. The signature and
  the default call are unchanged, and the centering is always on. Sequence-level
  corrections still multiply the advantage, and the per-token centering applies
  on top. Metrics are unchanged.

Sanity checks:

* On policy, the gradient equals the original loss'"'"'s gradient (max difference 7e-9).
* CPU replica, noise 0.3, 600 steps, `plus_minus`, 100 extra tail tokens:

  | Loss | Reward |
  | --- | --- |
  | Original PG | collapses to 0 (2 of 2 seeds) |
  | New loss | eval reward 0.79–0.80 (3 seeds) |

* Default dev setting: final train reward 0.85 vs 0.58 for the baseline.

## Configuration

No configuration changes are needed. The centering is active with default
arguments and `rl.is.level=null`.

Falling reward makes ā more negative, which speeds it up, and that feedback is the collapse. IS corrections leave a remainder m − (Σm)p, where m = q·w(p/q). That remainder is zero only for untruncated IS (w = p/q), so clipping leaves the bias in place and tighter bands can make it worse.

**The fix.** Each token's term becomes `w·log p(y_t) − Σ_v sg(m(v))·log p(v)`, with m = q when no correction is given.
- It is computed exactly on the sampler's top-20 tokens, which the batch already provides. The rest of the sampler's probability is pooled as one term, assuming it is spread in proportion to p.
- With a correction, m uses the same `log_mass` function the correction uses, so it stays exact for TIS, MIS, PPO, DPPO and the others.
- Without the top-20 data and without a correction, it falls back to unclipped token-level IS, which also gives a zero-mean score. Without the top-20 data but with a correction, the sum covers only the sampled token, and the rest is pooled.

**Why it works.** The subtracted term is exactly the expected value under q of the first term, so the score averages to zero in every state. The drift term is removed for any type of mismatch. What remains is the reward signal, Σ_v q(v)(A(v) − Ā_q)e_v. When q = p the change adds nothing: the gradient matches the original loss to 7e-9. The subtracted term is computed exactly, not sampled, so it adds no heavy-tailed weights. `REPORT.md` has the full derivation.

**Test results (`dev/mini.py`, 600 steps):**

| Setting | Original loss | New loss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default dev setting (`./run_dev.sh`) | final train reward 0.58 | 0.85 |
| 100 extra unlikely tokens, plus/minus rewards | collapses to 0 (2 seeds) | eval reward 0.79–0.80 (3 seeds) |
| Same, group-centred rewards | about 0.75 eval | about 0.72 eval |
| Same, with TIS | about the same as the new loss | about the same as the original |

So in the group-centred and TIS settings the original already works and the new loss gives no gain. In group-centred mode it trails a little, on a single seed.

The fallback without top-20 data matches naive IS. My first fallback, which centred on the sampled token only, collapsed. In the final version that approach is used only when a correction is given and the top-20 data is missing, and I did not test that case.
